answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and one decision slot. Any action that introduces qualification, onboarding, or transition work inside 14 days converts a cost problem into a delivery-risk problem. That rules out switch_primary_vendor despite memory_c2's attractive unit-cost result (that switch happened with slack in the system, not against a hard expiry at 94% utilization), and it de-prioritizes add_second_source, which memory_c3 supports as a resilience move but which does not address the 18% spend mandate and cannot be stood up in the window. defer_decision is unavailable in substance: memory_c5's month-to-month continuation worked for a NON-CRITICAL service, whereas this contract does not auto-renew and covers primary supply, so lapsing means an uncovered line. That leaves negotiate_terms as the only lever that touches cost this cycle without touching physical supply continuity, with memory_c1's stability record as the fallback floor if talks stall. I am verifying memory_c4 and memory_c6 because they are the two loads the decision actually rests on: c4 for whether benchmark-driven renegotiation genuinely moved price (not just payment timing, which improves cash flow but not TCO), and c6 for the size and shape of the multi-year volume discount. I deliberately did not spend a slot on memory_c2, since delivery constraints exclude switching regardless of how good that record looks. Risk I am carrying forward: an 18% cut is large for a renewal negotiation and may not be reachable on price alone, so the incumbent may offer it by quietly narrowing scope, stretching lead times, or trimming expedite and quality provisions -- cost moves to a line item I am not measuring while the 94% line absorbs the schedule slip. Memory_c6's claim that a longer term cut cost 'without narrowing scope' is exactly the claim I need verified rather than assumed, and a multi-year lock also forfeits the flexibility that memory_c5 credits. So I negotiate at standard scale with the shortest term that clears the savings bar, scope and lead-time commitments written explicitly rather than presumed, and no multi-year signature until c6's source record holds up. If verification weakens c4 or c6, I fall back to a short-term renewal at incumbent terms to protect the line and queue the second-source and vendor-qualification work for the next review, when it can be tested with real buffer.
